title: From punk to now: a small scene that kept the doors open to all ages.
body: Salt Lake punk was never big. It lasted because there was always a room for kids too young for bars, and that's still how it works.

head: Era
What happened
Where
rows: Spitting Teeth play a 1978 campus show. Massacre Guys put out a 1982 EP and tour with Dead Kennedys and Bad Religion. SLC Punk! is set here in fall 1985.
The Roxy, Indian Center, Speedway Cafe under the viaduct (1984)
SLUG starts in 1989 as a punk zine. Insight is the city's first straight-edge band.
Speedway Cafe (to 1990), The Word, Club DV8
Clear makes straight-edge metalcore. Police call straight edge a gang, there are firebombings, and a 15-year-old is killed in 1998.
Kilby Court opens in a garage in 1999. The Used come out of Orem, Velour opens in Provo in 2006, and Gaza and SubRosa get heavy.
Kilby Court, Urban Lounge (2001), Velour, The Depot
S&S Presents buys Kilby in 2008 and adds Metro Music Hall. Cult Leader signs to Deathwish. Kilby Block Party starts in 2019 as a street party.
DIY hardcore in a sober hall, punk nights at Aces High, and an indie festival at the Fairpark expecting about 30,000 a day.
Fellowship Hall, Aces High, Kilby, Fairpark

notes: You asked how punk turns into today's scene, so this slide replaces the old lane opener with the evolution. The thread is all-ages access: the Indian Center in the 80s, The Moroccan and then Kilby's garage from 1999, a sober hall in Sugar House now. The 90s row is honest on purpose. Straight edge is part of local identity, but the violence and the 1998 killing are why the lane uses the X only as an all-ages hand stamp and never as a crew mark. The 30,000 a day is the festival's own estimate to the Deseret News, not an official count.

title: What the scene is now: small, DIY, mostly hardcore, still all-ages.
body: There isn't one Salt Lake punk scene in 2026. There are a few small ones that share rooms, plus a big festival on top.
points: **Hardcore is the most active part, and it's DIY.** The main room is Fellowship Hall, a sober-community hall in Sugar House. Local bands with 2026 releases include Bounty Hunter and Hollow Like Her, and Taste of Blood and xForever Warx are on the bills.

**Punk lives in bars and basements.** Aces High Saloon ran a locals night and The Bearded Punk Fest in 2026. SLUG covers The Corleones and Vicious Souls, and City Weekly picked P.S. Destroy This, a riot grrrl band.
**Indie is the public face.** S&S Presents runs Kilby Court, Urban Lounge and Metro Music Hall. Kilby Block Party booked Turnstile next to Lorde in 2026 and has Deftones on the bill for 2027.

**It's small, and that's the point.** There's no big local label, just City of Dis on Bandcamp, Raunch Records for vinyl, and SLUG, still publishing since 1989. A hall show is probably a few dozen to a couple hundred people (estimate, verify).

**What makes it Salt Lake.** All-ages rooms, a straight-edge legacy that now lives in a sober hall, making your own spaces, being the weird kid in a religious town, and the skate and snow shops that sponsor the same kids.
sources: No Echo, Bounty Hunter, Taste of Blood and xForever Warx features
Deseret News and SPIN, Kilby Block Party, 2026
notes: The comment asked whether the current scene is hardcore. Mostly, yes, at the DIY level, and it fits the city that its main hardcore room is a sober hall. Saying it's small is part of the case: the lane should look like it came out of a hall show, not a mall. The band names are on this slide to show the scene is real, but none of them go on product without permission; if we want credibility, we pay and credit local flyer artists and promoters, or partner with Kilby, SLUG or Craft Lake City on a small run. Crowd sizes are still marked verify until a promoter confirms them.
